slides.text: Welcome to lectures seven and eight: numerical and categorical variables, non-graphical versus graphical E D A. We apply every technique to every feature of one large real dataset, the Superstore retail orders.

Our dataset has eight thousand three hundred ninety nine real retail orders for office supplies, technology and furniture, with full sales, discount and shipping detail. Everyone understands buying something online, and unlike Titanic or Iris, most students have never analysed it. We separate non-graphical, statistical E D A from graphical, visual E D A, apply both to every feature, then compare. Numbers first for precision, plots second for shape, then check that the two agree.

There are six numerical features. Sales is the dollar value of the order. Profit is the dollar profit or loss, and it can be negative. Discount is the rate, from zero to about twenty five percent. Order quantity runs from one to fifty units. Unit price is the price of a single unit before discount. And shipping cost is the dollar cost of shipping.

And three categorical features. Product category: office supplies, technology or furniture. Ship mode: regular air, delivery truck or express air. And customer segment: consumer, corporate, home office or small business. Together they describe what was bought, how it shipped, and who bought it.
The very first non-graphical check on any dataset is counting empty cells, before any statistic or plot. One line does it for every column at once: df dot isna dot sum.

Product base margin is missing for sixty three orders, just zero point seven five percent, a small and easily flagged gap. Every one of the six numerical features we use today has zero missing values, and the categorical features are complete too.

Technique one is central tendency. The mean is the arithmetic average and is sensitive to extremes. The median is the middle value and resists extremes. The mode is the most frequent value. Each is one line for all numerical columns: mean, median, mode, no loop needed.

Profit shows the most dramatic gap of any feature: the mean is one hundred eighty one dollars while the median is minus one fifty. The average and the typical order tell opposite stories. Order quantity and discount have mean and median close together. And sales and unit price have a mean far above the median, a first hint of strong right skew.

Technique two is dispersion. Standard deviation is the typical spread from the mean. Range is maximum minus minimum and is sensitive to one extreme value. The I Q R is Q three minus Q one, the spread of the middle fifty percent, and resists extremes. Again one line computes each statistic for every feature.

Sales has a standard deviation of thirty five eighty five, more than twice its I Q R of fifteen sixty six. A handful of very large orders are stretching the spread. Profit's standard deviation is over four times its I Q R, the same pattern for gains and losses. Order quantity's standard deviation and I Q R are in sensible proportion: well-behaved dispersion.

Technique three is shape. Skewness of zero means symmetric, positive means a long right tail, and the further from zero the more lopsided. Kurtosis measures how heavy the tails are: very high kurtosis means extreme values are far more common than a normal distribution predicts. Skew and kurtosis are one line each for every feature.

Unit price is extraordinarily skewed, fourteen point one three, with kurtosis of two seventy one, the most extreme feature. Sales, skew five point four, and profit, skew three point six five, are also dramatically skewed. Order quantity and discount sit almost exactly at zero, genuinely symmetric.

Ranked by skewness, unit price towers over every other feature, so extreme that it barely fits on the same chart. Order quantity and discount sit at zero. The numbers tell us sales, profit and unit price are wildly skewed, but they cannot show us what that shape looks like. For that we need pictures.
